title: Refresh token grace period is perpetually extensible, defeating token-theft detection
description: When a rotated (revoked) refresh token is reused within the 60-second grace window, the rotateToken() method overwrites rotated_at with the current timestamp, effectively resetting the grace period. An attacker who intercepts a refresh token can keep reusing it indefinitely by sending requests within each 60-second window. Each successful reuse resets rotated_at to now, so the revoked-token-reuse detection (revokeAllUserTokens) never triggers. The attacker maintains persistent access while the legitimate user is unaware.
impact: An attacker who steals a single refresh token gains indefinite session persistence. The token-theft detection mechanism (revoking all user tokens when a revoked token is reused outside the grace period) is completely bypassed because the grace window resets on each reuse. The attacker can continuously generate new access tokens and refresh tokens in parallel with the legitimate user.
attack_path: 1. Attacker intercepts refresh token T via network sniffing, XSS, or log exposure. 2. Legitimate user uses T to refresh, obtaining new tokens. T is marked revoked with rotated_at=T1. 3. Within 60s, attacker sends T to POST /api/auth/refresh. validateToken() passes the grace check (Date.now() - T1 < 60000). 4. rotateToken() updates rotated_at to T2=now, resetting the grace window. Attacker gets new valid tokens. 5. Within 60s of T2, attacker repeats step 3. The grace window resets to T3. 6. This loop continues indefinitely, giving the attacker permanent access.
evidence: auth/infrastructure/services/refresh-token.service.ts:56-62 (grace period check uses rotated_at which is overwritten on each reuse)
auth/infrastructure/services/refresh-token.service.ts:83-92 (rotateToken overwrites rotated_at with new Date(), resetting the grace window)
auth/application/use-cases/refresh-tokens.use-case.ts:22-30 (validateToken then rotateToken sequence without preventing grace period reset)
remediation: Record the original rotated_at timestamp and do not overwrite it when the token is reused within the grace period. Alternatively, track a 'used_within_grace' flag and reject any second reuse of the same rotated token. A safer approach: return the previously-issued new token from a cache during the grace window instead of generating a fresh one, and mark the rotated token as fully consumed after first grace-period reuse so a second reuse triggers revokeAllUserTokens.

title: Refresh token hashing defeated by plaintext fallback lookup enabling use of stolen DB hashes as valid tokens
description: The validateToken(), revokeToken(), and rotateToken() methods all fall back to querying the database by the raw token value when the hashed lookup fails. Since generateToken() stores the SHA-256 hash in the 'token' column, an attacker who obtains database contents (via SQL injection, backup exposure, or DB compromise) can use the stored hash values directly as refresh tokens. The fallback lookup will match the stored hash against the provided raw value, bypassing the hashing protection entirely.
impact: Complete compromise of all active refresh token sessions upon database exposure. The SHA-256 hashing layer, which is supposed to prevent token recovery from stored hashes, provides zero protection. An attacker with read access to the refresh_tokens table can impersonate any user with an active refresh token.
attack_path: 1. Attacker gains read access to the refresh_tokens table (e.g., SQL injection, leaked backup, compromised DB credentials). 2. Attacker extracts stored hash H from the 'token' column for an active (non-revoked, non-expired) token. 3. Attacker sends H as the refresh_token to POST /api/auth/refresh. 4. validateToken(H): computes hash(H)=H2, looks up by H2 → not found. Falls back to looking up by raw value H → matches the DB row. 5. Token validation succeeds. Attacker receives new access + refresh tokens for the victim user.
evidence: auth/infrastructure/services/refresh-token.service.ts:37-49 (validateToken falls back to findOne({where: {token}}) with raw value after hash lookup fails)
auth/infrastructure/services/refresh-token.service.ts:20-35 (generateToken stores hash in token column: token: hashRefreshToken(token))
remediation: Remove the plaintext fallback lookup entirely. If backward compatibility with pre-hashing tokens is still needed, run a one-time migration to hash all existing plaintext tokens in the database, then remove the fallback code. Alternatively, add a 'hash_version' column to distinguish legacy plaintext tokens and only allow the fallback for rows explicitly marked as unhashed.

title: Password reset endpoint lacks password complexity validation allowing weak passwords
description: The ResetPasswordDto only enforces MinLength(8) on the newPassword field but does not apply the @IsPassword() decorator or MaxLength validation. In contrast, RegisterDto and ChangePasswordDto both enforce @IsPassword() (which requires uppercase and lowercase characters) and MaxLength(100). An attacker who compromises a password reset flow can set an arbitrarily simple 8-character password (e.g., 'aaaaaaaa') that would not be accepted through normal registration or password change.
impact: Users who reset their passwords can set weak passwords that bypass the complexity requirements enforced everywhere else. This creates accounts with passwords vulnerable to brute-force and dictionary attacks. The inconsistency also means password policy is not uniformly enforced.
attack_path: 1. Attacker initiates password reset for a target account via POST /api/auth/request-password-reset. 2. Attacker obtains the SMS reset code (via social engineering, SIM swap, or if this is the target's own account). 3. Attacker calls POST /api/auth/reset-password with newPassword='aaaaaaaa' (8 lowercase chars, no uppercase, no special chars). 4. Password is accepted because ResetPasswordDto only checks MinLength(8). 5. The same password 'aaaaaaaa' would be rejected by RegisterDto or ChangePasswordDto which require @IsPassword() complexity.
remediation: Add the @IsPassword() and @MaxLength(100) decorators to the newPassword field in ResetPasswordDto to match the validation applied in RegisterDto and ChangePasswordDto.

title: Unauthenticated E2E endpoint creates fully-privileged accounts when NODE_ENV is misconfigured
description: The POST /api/auth/e2e/google-business-user endpoint has no authentication guard (no JwtAuthGuard, no AdminGuard). It relies solely on the NODE_ENV environment variable check inside the use case (blocking only 'production' and 'stage'). If NODE_ENV is undefined, empty, or set to any value other than 'production'/'stage' (e.g., 'prod', 'Production', 'staging'), the endpoint allows any anonymous HTTP client to create fully authenticated business accounts with valid JWT and refresh tokens.
impact: In any environment where NODE_ENV is not exactly 'production' or 'stage', an anonymous attacker can create unlimited authenticated business user accounts. Each call returns valid access and refresh tokens without requiring email, phone verification, or password. This could be exploited if a preview/staging/development deployment is accessible from the internet.
attack_path: 1. Attacker discovers a non-production deployment (e.g., preview environment, development server exposed via ngrok, or a deployment where NODE_ENV is misconfigured). 2. Attacker sends POST /api/auth/e2e/google-business-user with no authentication headers. 3. The use case checks process.env.NODE_ENV - if it's not 'production' or 'stage', assertAllowed() passes. 4. A new Business user is created with a verified email and phone. 5. Access and refresh tokens are returned in cookies. 6. Attacker now has a fully authenticated account that can create listings, access all authenticated features.
evidence: auth/application/use-cases/e2e-create-google-business-user.use-case.ts:24-29 (assertAllowed only blocks 'production' and 'stage', undefined/other values pass)
auth/application/use-cases/e2e-create-google-business-user.use-case.ts:31-63 (creates user with phoneVerified:true, emailVerified:true, returns full login response)
remediation: Apply a defense-in-depth approach: 1) Use an allowlist instead of a denylist - only allow the endpoint when NODE_ENV is exactly 'development' or 'test'. 2) Add an additional secret-based guard (e.g., require a header with a shared E2E secret). 3) Consider gating the route registration itself behind the environment check so the endpoint is not even mounted in non-development builds.
